paragraphs.text: Today on Hey, Flag!, we have three special guests from North America.
Hey, Flag! Tell us about yourself.
"I am the Mexican flag. I have three stripes. The Mexican coat of arms is in the middle. The coat of arms has a very special meaning. It symbolizes the Aztec people who lived in Mexico long ago.
"The coat of arms shows an eagle sitting on a cactus. The eagle is eating a snake. This symbol came from an Aztec legend. The legend tells how Mexico City was founded.

"There is a funny story about my red stripe. Originally the Mexican people wanted to use purple. Purple represented Spain, where most of Mexico's people came from. But they could not find any purple cloth. So they had to use red."
Hey, Flag! Tell us about yourself.

"I am the flag of the United States of America. Many people call me the Stars and Stripes. I have fifty stars, one for each of the states. I also have thirteen stripes for each of the original states. I didn't always have fifty stars. Every time a new state was added, I got another star.
"Many people believe I was first sewn by Betsy Ross. According to the story, George Washington asked Betsy to sew me.
"The first flag was ready in early June 1776. This was just a month before the United States became an independent country.
"Many Americans see me as the greatest symbol of their nation."
Hey, Flag! Tell us about yourself.

"I am the Canadian flag. You can call me the Maple Leaf. I did not become the Canadian flag until 1965. Before that, Canadians used the flag of Great Britain. But the people of Canada wanted to have their own flag.
"The maple leaf has been a symbol of Canada for a very long time. In 1860 the Prince of Wales came to Canada for a visit. Everyone in Toronto came out into the streets to greet him.

"The people who were born in England wore a rose on their shirts. And the people born in Scotland wore a thistle. But there was nothing for the people born in Canada to wear. So they chose to wear a maple leaf from the Canadian maple tree.
"From that day on, the maple leaf became a Canadian symbol."
I hope you learned a lot from our guests. Your flag can tell you a lot about your country. What does your flag mean?
Once upon a time, there was a kindhearted girl. Her evil stepmother would not let her go to the prince's ball. But a fairy godmother came to the rescue.
Can you guess what story this is? Here's a hint: there is a glass shoe. That's right! The story is "Cinderella."
"Cinderella" is a very old fairy tale. In fact, it's over a thousand years old. But the glass shoe and the fairy godmother only appeared around three hundred years ago.

This version of "Cinderella" was published in France in 1697. It introduced most of the details that are familiar today. A pumpkin becomes a carriage. Mice are turned into horses. And the fairy godmother's magic wears off at midnight. But this version is very different from earlier "Cinderella" stories.

One of the earliest known "Cinderella" stories appeared in China around 860. In this story Cinderella wants to go to a festival and not a ball. And instead of a fairy godmother, there is a magic fish. Cinderella wears a gown made of sea green silk. Her cloak is made of feathers. And her lost shoe is made of gold.

Much later a story called "Kongjwi and Patjwi" was written. This one comes from Korea. Kongjwi has an evil stepmother and a stepsister named Patjwi. The stepmother gives Kongjwi lots of chores so she cannot go to a feast. A bull, a toad, sparrows, and a fairy all help Kongjwi finish the chores. On Kongjwi's way to the feast, she loses her silk shoe in a stream. The local governor finds the lost shoe. He searches for its owner and finds Kongjwi at the feast.

In 1634 the first European version of the story was published in Italy. A fairy lives in a date tree over the grave of Cinderella's mother. The fairy helps Cinderella attend a ball. When she loses her shoe, the king finds it. To find the shoe's owner, he invites the women of the kingdom to a feast. At the feast the shoe jumps out of the king's hands. It flies onto Cinderella's foot!
Today even more versions of "Cinderella" exist. Each story has different details. But the storyline usually follows the same pattern with a missing shoe.
Can you guess how the story almost always ends? Yes—Cinderella and her husband live "happily ever after!"
Lara and Mom walked along a canal. Mom read aloud from her Venice guidebook. But Lara was too excited to listen.
"This is the Rialto Bridge," read Mom. "It is the oldest bridge on the Grand Canal and—"
"Ooh!" Lara squealed. She pointed to a row of black boats. "Mom, can we take a gondola ride?"
"Good idea," said Mom. "My feet are getting sore."
Mom hired a gondola to go to St. Mark's Square. Marco, the driver, helped them into the boat. Lara and Mom sat down on the pretty red cushions.

Marco gestured with one arm and rowed with the other. "This is the Grand Canal. It's one of the major waterways in Venice," he said. "It's almost four kilometers long. And it's ninety meters wide in some places. There are 177 canals in Venice."
A long motorboat passed by.
"That looks like a bus!" said Lara.
"That's a water bus," said Marco. "We don't have cars in Venice. So people have to walk. Or they travel on the canals. We have water buses and even water taxis!" He pointed to a smaller motorboat.
Marco steered the gondola into a narrow canal.
"There's less traffic in this canal," Lara said. She stared up at the tall, elegant buildings.
"Venice was a rich and powerful city during the Renaissance," Marco said. "People built palace-like houses to show off their wealth."
They passed under a covered white bridge.
"The Doge's Palace is on the right," Marco said. It was a beautiful white building.
Lara wrinkled her nose. "What's a doge?" she asked.
"The doge was the ruler of Venice," Marco said. "The palace is a museum now."
At the end of the canal, Marco turned the gondola into an open lagoon.
"Here we are," announced Marco. "This is St. Mark's Square!"
Marco helped Mom and Lara out of the gondola.
"Can we go see the Doge's Palace, Mom?" asked Lara.
"Be sure to see St. Mark's Church and the bell tower too!" Marco said.
"Thank you," said Mom. She turned to Lara. "My feet feel rested now. I'm ready for more sightseeing."
Lara cheered. "Good! Let's go!"
Today on Hey, Flag! , we have three special guests from Europe.
Hey, Flag! Tell us about yourself!
"I am the flag of Denmark. Called the Dannebrog, I am over eight-hundred years old.

"Legend says I fell from heaven. In the thirteenth century, King Valdemar II was fighting a battle—and losing. Suddenly a red banner with a white cross fell from the sky. The king and the Danish army thought my sudden appearance was a sign from God. Everyone was filled with courage to fight even harder, and the Danes won the battle.

"Ever since then, I have been an important symbol to the Danish people. People proudly fly me on June 15, Valdemar's Day, to celebrate my miraculous appearance. But that's not the only day Danes celebrate me. People often decorate birthday cakes and Christmas trees with my image too.
"Before I go, I have something else to brag about. My design inspired the flags of other Nordic countries. Finland, Sweden, Norway, and Iceland all have cross designs too."
Hey, Flag! Tell us about yourself!
"I am the Union Jack, the flag of the United Kingdom. My design comes from the different countries that make up the UK. I am one of the most recognizable flags in the world.

"A long time ago, England and Scotland were separate kingdoms with different flags. In England, St. George's Cross was on the flag. This is a red cross on a white background called a field. In Scotland, St. Andrew's Cross was on the flag. This is a diagonal white cross on a blue field.
"In 1603 King James of Scotland became the king of England, uniting the two kingdoms. He wanted a new flag to represent this union. That's when I was created!

"Almost two centuries later, I was redesigned because Ireland became part of the United Kingdom. St. Patrick is an important saint to Ireland. So St. Patrick's Cross was added to my design. This is a diagonal red cross on a white field. Though only Northern Ireland is in the UK today, my design has stayed the same.
"You may have seen me on the flags of Australia and New Zealand. In fact, I appear on the flags of several other countries and places.
Hey, Flag! Tell us about yourself!

"My name is the Tricolore, which means three colors. I am the flag of France. I was created around 1789 during the French Revolution. That's when the French people removed their monarchy and set up the First French Republic. My design was seen to represent the ideals of the revolution: liberty, equality, and fraternity.

"Why do I have red, white, and blue stripes? No one knows for sure! But people who supported the revolution wore red, white, and blue ribbons. And the colors do have other historical meanings. Red and blue are the colors of Paris, the capital of France. Red is associated with St. Denis, the protector of Paris. And blue is linked to St. Martin, who was known for helping the poor.
"Some people think my white stripe represents the nation. Others think it recognizes the old monarchy's white royal flag.

"After I was officially adopted in 1794, France's politics remained stormy. Two decades later, France had a king again. I was replaced for a while by the white royal flag. I returned in 1830. Apart from a few days, I've proudly been the flag of France ever since."
I hope you learned a lot from our guests. Your flag has a rich history. What does your flag mean?
One day my little sister, Sarah, kept wiggling her tooth.
"Mommy, I have a loose tooth!" she said.
"Do you know who comes when a tooth falls out?" I said.
"Who?" Sarah asked.
"A tooth robber!" I said.
"Owen! Stop teasing her," Mom said.
Sarah still looked confused. "Who will come when my tooth falls out?"
"The tooth fairy," Mom said.
"A fairy? What does the tooth fairy do?" Sarah asked.
"Oh, I can't tell you. You'll see," Mom said.
"I want my tooth to fall out now!" Sarah stuck her tongue under her tooth. She wiggled the tooth, but it didn't fall out. Then she yanked on it with one, two, three fingers.
"Ugh!" she moaned.
I grinned. "I can get your tooth out. I'll tie it to a door with string. Then I'll slam the door!"
"No!" Sarah ran away.
"Owen!" Mom sighed. "That's not helpful. Stop teasing her."
For the next few days, Sarah kept wiggling her tooth. But the tooth didn't come out.
One afternoon she looked sad. "This tooth is never going to come out!"
"I have an idea," I said.
She looked at me suspiciously. "What is it?"
I handed her an apple. "Take a bite of this."
"Owen, are you teasing me again?" Sarah asked.
"Of course not," I said. "I never tease you!"
Sarah still looked unsure, but she bit into the apple. "My tooth fell out!"
"Where is it?" I asked.
She held out the apple.
We both laughed. The tooth was stuck in the apple!
"Put it under your pillow for the tooth fairy tonight," I said.
The next morning a loud cry came from Sarah's room. "Mom! Owen! Come see!"
"Did the tooth fairy come?" Mom asked her.
"Yes!" Sarah said. She lifted up her pillow. "My tooth is gone. And there's money instead!"
"Congratulations on your first visit from the tooth fairy," I said.
Sarah grinned. "Hooray for the tooth fairy, and . . ." She smiled widely and pointed to her missing tooth. "Hooray for Owen!"
"Let's go fishing," Dad said one day. "I'll teach you how to fish."
"Yes!" I cried.
Dad and I drove to a shop. We bought hooks, floats, and worms for bait. We also bought fishing line for our rods.
Then we headed to the river.
Dad pointed to a small motorboat at a dock. "That's our boat!"
The boat rocked as we climbed in. Dad started the motor. Vroom!
Finally we stopped in the middle of the river.
"Time to fish!" Dad said.
He helped me tie a hook and float to my fishing rod. Then I looked at the tub of bait. I picked out the biggest worm.
"Dad, let's put this one on my hook. I'll catch a huge fish!"
Dad smiled. "We'll see!"
He showed me how to cast the line into the water. "Now we must wait for the fish to bite," he said.
We waited and waited. But the fish did not bite!
"Look!" Dad said suddenly.
The float on my line was bobbing up and down!
Dad helped me reel in the line.
I grinned. "I caught a fish! Now I'm a real fisherman!"
"Yes, you are!" Dad said. "But this fish is too small to keep. We have to toss it back."
"Ugh," I groaned. We let the fish go, and it quickly swam away.
Soon I cast out the line again. The air grew cold as we waited some more.
"Dad, I'm cold," I said. "And bored."
Dad nodded. "Fishermen do a lot of waiting!"
Just then a big boat passed by.
"Maybe we can fish on a boat like that someday," Dad said. "We can fish on the ocean and catch all kinds of fish. Really big ones."
"Thanks," I said. "But fishing is boring. I'm not sure—"
"Look!" Dad cried.
My line was bobbing again! This time I reeled it in by myself.
"You caught a big, beautiful trout!" Dad said.
I was so proud. "Dad, can we go fishing again tomorrow?"
Dad laughed. "I thought you didn't like fishing!"
I shook my head. "I love it!"
Sanjay was in the kitchen when his sister, Priya, ran by. She had a bundle of markers and several pieces of cardboard. The next time she went by, she had a Betsy doll and a Space Man figure.
"That's my Space Man!" Sanjay said. "What are you doing, Priya?" He followed her into the family room.
"I was watching videos on the Internet," Priya said. "I saw a film that a kid made and decided to make one myself."
Sanjay's eyes lit up. "You'll need actors! Can I be in your movie?"
Priya shook her head. "I don't need actors. This is going to be a stop-motion animation."
"Animation?" Sanjay asked.

"I'm going to take lots of pictures of Betsy and Space Man. I'll move them a little between each picture," Priya explained. "When I put all the pictures together, it will look like they're moving! Want to help?"
"Sure."
Sanjay helped Priya color buildings on a piece of cardboard.
"This will be the background," Priya said. "Betsy is going to chase Space Man."
"Why is she going to chase him?" Sanjay asked.
Priya shrugged.
Sanjay laughed. "Priya, she needs to have a reason for chasing him. If she doesn't, the film won't be interesting. Let's come up with a story with a beginning, middle, and end."
Priya and Sanjay thought.
"Okay," Priya said. "Betsy puts down her favorite marker. When she isn't looking, it rolls away and Space Man finds it. He picks it up and—"
"Betsy thinks he stole the marker," Sanjay added, "so she chases him!"
Priya smiled. "Perfect! Then he falls down and she takes back the marker. The end!"
Sanjay set up the cardboard background. He placed paper and a marker in front of Betsy. Priya got the camera ready.

Priya took a picture of Betsy with the marker. Then Sanjay moved Betsy's hand, just a tiny bit. Priya took another picture. After a long time, they had a bunch of pictures. They uploaded the pictures to a filmmaking program on Priya's laptop. The program quickly showed all the pictures, one at a time.
"Cool!" Sanjay said. "It looks like Betsy is drawing with the marker!"
Next they filmed the marker rolling away from Betsy. Then they took pictures of Space Man picking up the marker.
"Now we film the big chase scene," Priya said. They spent all afternoon moving Betsy and Space Man tiny little bits at a time.

They uploaded the rest of the pictures to the laptop. Sanjay and Priya recorded voices for Space Man and Betsy. Then they added some music. When they were finished, they showed the movie to their parents.
"Let's upload this to the Internet," Priya said after the movie.
Sanjay grinned. "Maybe it will inspire other kids to make movies too!"
Grace gazed at the big painting of a dancer.
"That's beautiful!" she said. "When I get older, I want to be an artist."
Grace and Dad were at an art museum in Boston. Grace suddenly noticed an empty frame on a wall. Then she noticed another empty frame.
"Dad?" Grace asked. "Why are those frames empty?"
"Their paintings are missing," said Dad. "Actually someone stole them."
She gasped. "Really?"
A museum guard walked over. "It was the biggest art theft in American history," he said.
"When did it happen?" Grace asked.

"March 18, 1990," said the guard. "Two thieves came late at night. They were dressed as police officers. So a museum guard let the men inside. The thieves stole paintings, sketches, a bronze eagle, and a small vase. All together the items are worth about fifty million dollars."
"Whoa," said Grace. "That's a lot of money. I guess the thieves knew what to steal!"
"The men did steal some valuable artwork," said the guard. "But they left more valuable artwork behind. Many people think the thieves didn't know much about art."
"Were the men ever caught?" asked Grace's dad.

The guard shook his head. "The police had several suspects. But they never caught anyone. Workers at the museum decided to hang four empty frames. The frames remind everyone of the stolen paintings. We hope to get them back someday."
Grace looked at Dad. "I don't want to be an artist anymore. I want to be a detective. And I want to solve this case!"

"I'm done!" It was Wednesday night, and Lily had just finished typing her report on icebergs. For a moment she was relieved. But then her heart sank. On Friday she would have to stand in front of her class and present the report. She hated speaking in public. What if she made a fool of herself?
On Thursday Lily was talking with her friends. "The Green Guys are coming to our school tomorrow," Sandeep said.
The Green Guys were a theater group. They acted, played music, and performed magic tricks.

"That will be fun," Lily said. Then her stomach did a flip. Tomorrow was Friday—she had to present her iceberg report to the class. "I'll be so nervous that I won't be able to enjoy the Green Guys at all," she thought.

That night Lily practiced reading her report. She hated the sound of her voice, and at one point, she said "icebug" instead of "iceberg." She groaned. "I'm going to make so many mistakes. Everyone is going to laugh at me."
Lily watched some public speaking tutorials online. They all said basically the same thing: be prepared, be relaxed, and be confident.
In the morning Lily's stomach was in knots. "Maybe the school bus will get a flat tire," she thought. "Then I won't have to go to school."
An hour later Lily was in the school auditorium. Everyone laughed as the Green Guys did a silly dance. Even Lily was enjoying the show.
One Green Guy walked into the crowd of students. He needed a volunteer. All around Lily, kids raised their hands and shouted.
"I'll volunteer!"
"Pick me!"
Lily sank as low as she could, trying to be invisible. She gulped when the Green Guy looked directly at her and waved her over.
Lily wanted to escape. But everyone was staring at her. Reluctantly she followed the Green Guy up onto the stage.

The Green Guy handed Lily a jar of jelly beans and then ran to the other end of the stage. He opened his mouth and pointed at it. Lily threw one of the jelly beans, and the Green Guy caught it in his mouth. Everyone cheered.
Lily was amazed. She threw another jelly bean, and the Green Guy caught that one too. When Lily threw a third jelly bean, however, the Green Guy missed.
"Oops!" Lily thought. "He messed up!"
But the Green Guy didn't seem to care. He was already waiting for the next jelly bean. Lily quickly threw it. The Green Guy caught it, and everyone cheered again.
"He missed one," Lily thought, "and the audience barely noticed."

The jelly beans looked good, so Lily ate one. The Green Guy put his hands on his hips and pretended to be angry. Trying not to giggle, Lily pretended to be angry too. Everyone in the audience laughed.
"This is kind of fun," Lily thought.

Now the Green Guy was staring at her. He squinted as if he were wondering what Lily would do next. Lily stared back, grabbed a jelly bean, and ate it. The audience exploded with laughter as the Green Guy waved his arms around, pretending to be furious.
A moment later Lily and the Green Guy bowed. As Lily returned to her seat, everyone applauded and cheered for her.
Sandeep clapped her on the back. "You were awesome!"
Lily beamed. She thought about her presentation on icebergs and realized something: she wasn't nervous about making a mistake anymore!
Winn's fingers flew. The little cube in his hands twisted and turned. Bright, colorful squares moved at a rapid pace.
"Oh, a Rubik's Cube puzzle!" said Anika. "I just got one for my birthday."

"I'm trying to solve it quickly," said Winn. He stopped turning the cube and studied it for a moment. Then he turned the top layer clockwise and studied it again. Finally he sighed and set the puzzle on the table.
"I wish I'd invented the Rubik's Cube," he said. "Then I could solve it easily!"
Anika laughed. "I'm not so sure about that. It took the inventor a month to solve it the first time!"
"Really?" said Winn. "Who invented it?"
"A man named Erno Rubik," said Anika. "He was an architecture professor."
Winn scratched his head. "Why did he invent a toy?"

"Rubik didn't think of the cube as a toy at first," said Anika. "He invented it in 1974 to test out a design idea. But then he realized people really liked playing with the cube. He decided to manufacture and sell it."
"He sold a lot of them, right?" asked Winn.
"Rubik's Cube was extremely popular in the 1980s," said Anika. "Today it's still popular. In fact, it's one of the world's top-selling toys."
Winn grinned. "Well, someday I'm going to be the world's speed-cubing champion!"
"Oh, really?" asked Anika.

"Yep," said Winn. "There are speed-cubing competitions all over the world. The first world championship was held in 1982. People try to solve the Rubik's Cube as fast as they can. And there are different types of competitions too. Some people solve it with one hand. Others solve it blindfolded. Some people even solve it with their feet!"
Winn picked up the cube and started twisting it again. "A lot of people can solve it in less than ten seconds," he said.
"How fast are you?" asked Anika.
Winn gave a sheepish grin. "Actually, I haven't solved it at all yet."
"Don't feel bad," said Anika. "It's not easy to solve. There are billions of ways a Rubik's Cube can be scrambled."
Winn put the cube down again. "This is taking me forever!"
Anika picked up the cube and started twisting it. "A Rubik's Cube can always be solved in fewer than twenty moves."
"Impossible," said Winn.
"I'm serious," said Anika as she continued to move the sides around. "Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen . . . done!" Anika held out the Rubik's Cube.
Winn's eyes grew wide. "You solved it!"
"Here you go, Adriana." Grandpa handed me an apron and a cap. They looked silly with red, white, and green stripes. I gulped. Did I really have to wear them? What if someone from school saw me?

I didn't want to hurt Grandpa's feelings. He had spent the past year getting his pizzeria ready for business. Years ago he had been a pizzaiolo —a pizza maker—in Italy. Now he was finally going to make authentic Italian pizza here in America. His dream was coming true. But all I saw was a fashion nightmare.
"Pass out free slices of pizza Margherita to everyone who walks by," Grandpa instructed. "And be sure to tell them the story."

I grabbed a tray and started passing out pizza slices to people from a table set up outside. Then I saw them: Rachel and Clara—the most popular girls at my school. I pulled down my cap to hide my face. But it was too late.
"Hey, you're Adriana, from school, right?" Rachel said. "I didn't know there was a new pizza place in town."
Clara was looking around. "Don't you have pepperoni or Hawaiian pizza?"

"Oh! Hi!" I blurted out. I lifted my cap and started talking—much too fast. "Yes, my grandpa owns this place. Today's our grand opening. We don't serve American-style pizza, like pepperoni or Hawaiian. We only have pizza like they do in Italy. My grandpa wants it to be authentic."
"Awesome," Rachel said. "Can we try some?"
"Sure." I tried to act cool. I put two slices on plates and gave them to the girls.
"Mmm. Delicious!" Clara said.
Rachel nodded. "Much better than pepperoni pizza! What is this called?"

"It's called pizza Margherita. It was named after Queen Margherita. Back in 1889 in Italy, pizza was eaten mostly by workers who needed a quick lunch. But the queen was tired of fancy food. So she asked a pizza maker to make some pizzas. He made one with tomatoes, mozzarella cheese, and basil—the colors of the Italian flag! The queen loved it, and the pizza maker named the pizza after her. Soon everybody in Italy started eating pizza."
Rachel grinned. "We owe a big thanks to that Italian queen!"
"Can we try some other types of pizza?" Clara asked.
I got some more slices from the kitchen. "This is pizza bianca ," I said. "It's from Rome. There's no cheese—just olive oil and salt."
Next the girls tried the Sicilian-style pizza with anchovies—and they liked that too!
"My family is Italian American too," Rachel said. "But no one is good at cooking. You're so lucky your grandpa makes such great food."
I smiled. I felt proud of my family's culture—and Grandpa. When the girls left, I went back inside to get more of Grandpa's delicious pizza. And I didn’t even care about the apron or the cap anymore.
Daniel was eating lunch with his grandmother and her friends at the retirement community.
"Daniel does wonderful magic tricks," Grandma said proudly to Mr. Hudson and Mrs. Ross.
"Would you like to see one?" Daniel picked up his spoon and wiped it off. "I will now use my magic powers to bend this spoon."
Daniel focused on the spoon, which slowly bent in his hands.
"Such a clever boy!" Grandma said.
But Mr. Hudson wasn't impressed. "You need to work on concealing the spoon's handle. A magician must be aware of how his tricks look from every angle. I could see what you were doing over here."
Daniel sighed. "Are you a magician?"
Mr. Hudson nodded. "What's your favorite trick?"
Daniel's face lit up. "I love all kinds of magic, especially big illusions! It would be fun to make someone float above a table."

"Levitation tricks require special equipment that amateur magicians don't have," Mr. Hudson said. "Things like platforms that rise in the air. But I think card tricks and other close-up magic require more skill." He took out a coin. "My favorite tricks involve teleportation—like moving coins from place to place." Mr. Hudson made the coin vanish from one hand. He pulled it out from behind Daniel's ear with his other hand.
Daniel shook his head. "How did you do that?"
"Practice!" Mr. Hudson winked.
"I've always admired escape artists, though their routines make me so nervous," Mrs. Ross said. "Especially when someone is handcuffed or tied inside a tank of water."
"Don't worry," Mr. Hudson said. "An assistant slips the magician the keys to the handcuffs or uses knots that are easy to untie. The magician escapes quickly but stays underwater for suspense."
"I still wouldn't want Daniel trying that!" Grandma said. "I prefer classic tricks like pulling a rabbit out of a hat."
"Nobody does that anymore, Grandma. Using animals in magic acts is considered cruel. Magicians pull other things out of hats today—like bowling balls!"
"The item is often hidden in a secret compartment," Mr. Hudson explained. "The magician sets his hat over the compartment and pulls the object through an opening in the hat."
"I'm just a beginner," Daniel said. "All those tricks take lots of practice!"
Daniel was determined to outwit Mr. Hudson. So the next time he visited Grandma, he brought an assistant, his friend Joaquin.
"There's another kind of magic we didn't discuss," Daniel said as Joaquin blindfolded him. "Mind reading."
Joaquin invited Mrs. Ross to hand him any item from her purse. "I'm thinking about this object." Joaquin paused. "Read my mind."
"Wallet," Daniel said.
"You're right!" Mrs. Ross handed Joaquin something else.
"I'm thinking about this object." Joaquin paused for a few seconds. "Read my mind."
"Comb," Daniel replied.

"Wonderful!" Mr. Hudson applauded. "Magicians and their assistants usually have code words for different items, but I'm puzzled. Joaquin said the same thing both times. If you did the trick again, I could probably figure it out."
Daniel removed his blindfold. "That's why we're not repeating it!" he said.
"Won't you read my mind just once?" Grandma pleaded.
"Sure, that's easy." Daniel grinned. "You're thinking, 'Such a clever boy!'"
"I can't wait to try rock climbing!" Mason said. "It's going to be so much fun!"
Olivia bit her lip. "Um, yeah. I can't wait either."
Mason laughed. "You're not going to like rock climbing. You're afraid of heights, Olivia!"
"I am not!" Olivia folded her arms across her chest. She was terrified, but of course, she didn't want her brother to know that.
"We're here," Mom said as she pulled into the parking lot. "You two have fun."

Olivia and Mason went inside. An instructor asked the siblings for their shoe sizes. She grabbed a pair of rock-climbing shoes for each of them. After that she helped them put on harnesses and took them into the gym.
Olivia gasped. The walls were even taller than she'd expected. They were dotted with colorful objects that looked like rocks.
"What are those?" she asked.
"You use them to climb up the walls," the instructor said. "Different colors mark different routes. Some routes are more difficult than others."
"What do we do first?" Mason blurted out. "I'm ready to start!"
The instructor gave a short demonstration on how to climb.
"All of our walls have devices that control the rope as you climb," she said. "Just hook the rope onto your harness and climb. When you lean back, the device will lower you slowly."
"Awesome!" Mason ran to a wall, hooked a rope onto his harness, and started to climb. He looked down at his sister. "I'm going to beat you to the top!"

"Stop bragging!" Olivia said as she stepped up to the wall. She clipped the rope onto her harness. Carefully she placed her foot on a rock and got onto the wall. When she felt ready, she climbed a bit higher. She looked up at her brother, who was already halfway up the wall. "I can do this," she told herself. "I'm not scared."

Each time Olivia got a little higher, she took a deep breath. Then, when she felt comfortable, she climbed some more. She felt all of her muscles straining, but she enjoyed the feeling. In fact, she was starting to feel a lot less scared.
Soon she heard a bell ring from above.
"I'm at the top! I won!" Mason yelled. He looked down at Olivia with a sly grin. Suddenly his face went pale.
"Are you okay?" Olivia asked.
Mason was silent. His entire body was now flat against the wall.
"He went up too fast," Olivia thought. "He didn't realize how high he'd climbed."
Olivia continued up and was soon next to him.
Mason looked terrified. "H-how come you don't seem s-scared?" he asked his sister.
Olivia grinned. "I went up just a little bit at a time. That way, I got used to the height slowly. Now lean back. You'll be back on the floor soon."
Olivia led her brother down the wall. When Mason was ready, they climbed up again. This time he was a bit nervous. But Olivia wasn't scared at all!
This is my new guitar. It's extra special because I made it with my dad. He owns a business that makes and repairs guitars.

Stringed instruments have a long history. People in ancient Egypt and ancient Greece played plucked-string instruments. The first guitar was probably made in Spain in the sixteenth century. Early guitars had fewer strings and were shaped differently than today's guitars. Modern guitars have longer necks, and most have six strings. The top of the body is flat with a round hole in the middle.

Making the body was hard work, and it took a long time. First Dad let me pick out the wood. This is an important step since the wood helps make the sound. Woods like spruce and cedar are often used to make guitars. These woods are strong, and they vibrate easily. I chose a piece of spruce with a nice pattern in the wood. But this piece wasn't ready to cut yet. We had to dry it first. If the wood is not dry enough, it might shrink and crack after the guitar is made.

When the wood was ready, it was time for the next step. I traced outlines on the wood. Then Dad used a machine to cut out pieces for the sides, front, back, and neck. He did this part because the machines can be dangerous.

Have you ever wondered how a guitar's curved sides are made? Dad took the pieces for the sides and quickly dipped them in very hot water. This made the wood easy to bend. Then we had to clamp the pieces to a mold. This kept the wood bent as it dried.
While the sides were drying, we cut an opening in the neck for a long, thin piece of metal. The metal supports the neck and makes it strong.

The next step was gluing. We glued all the pieces tightly together, then left them to dry overnight. When the glue was dry, we sanded all the surfaces of the guitar to make them smooth. To protect the guitar, we brushed on several layers of protective coating. This also helped bring out the pattern in the wood. We had to wait overnight for each layer to dry.
The whole process took a long time, but today I finally attached the strings. My instrument was finished!

My guitar sounds great too! The strings vibrate when I pluck them, and this produces sound. The length of the string affects the sound. If the string is long, the sound is low. If it is short, the sound is high. When I play the guitar, I can press my finger on a string to make it shorter and change the sound. Frets help me know where to press to make the sound that I want. These are small strips of metal across the guitar's neck.

The strings alone don't make much sound. That's where the body of the guitar, or sound box, plays an important role. When a string is plucked over the hole in the sound box's top, the sound becomes louder. The strings vibrate the wood as well, also making the sound much louder.
Now my guitar is ready to play. I've even written a special song just for it. I can't wait to play it!
It was August 19—National Potato Day! The family was going to the Potato Festival.
"First, I'll drop off my potato soup for the cooking contest," said Dad. He took a big pot out of the car.
"Let's walk around while Dad goes to the judges' tent," said Mom.
At the first booth was a big world map.
"It says potatoes came from the Andes Mountains in South America," said Kate. "Early explorers took them to Europe and Asia."
"Potatoes kept thousands of Europeans from starving," said Mom.
"But look," said Seth, pointing at the map. "Europeans took potatoes to North America."
"Potatoes grow well in many places," said Mom. "They're one of the world's largest food crops."
"Enough geography," said Seth. "Let's eat!"
"We're waiting for Dad," said Kate.
They walked to another booth. A sign read: "What Can You Do with a Potato?"
"Wow! You can polish shoes and remove rust with potatoes," said Mom.
"This is cool," said Kate. "You can make glue."
"Look at this!" called Seth. They watched a man stick two pieces of metal into a potato. He connected wires to the metal pieces. A small lightbulb lit up!
"It's a potato battery," said Seth.
"A potato can power a small lightbulb for about forty days," said the man.
"Cool!" said Seth. "A potato costs a lot less than batteries!"
Seth's stomach growled.
"Sounds like you need to power up," said Mom. "There's Dad at the French fry booth."
They hurried over.
Dad grinned. "I'm discovering how to eat French fries."
"It's easy," said Seth. "You dip them in ketchup."
"In the Philippines they use banana ketchup," said Dad. "The English put vinegar on them. And in France they use mustard."
"Were French fries invented in France?" asked Kate.
"Nobody is sure," said Dad. "Thomas Jefferson first ate them in France. He loved them. He even served French fries at the White House."
Kate ordered curly fries and Seth got waffle fries. Mom and Dad got steak fries.
Seth licked ketchup from his fingers. "I'm full—until dinner."
Dad grinned and held up a blue ribbon. "Tonight we're having Dad's prize-winning potato soup!"
Grace was at the park. Today was her cousin's dragon boat race!
"I have to meet my team now," her cousin, Peter, said. "The race starts soon."
"Good luck!" said Grace.
Grace and Dad walked toward the river.
"Look!" Grace pointed to the boats on the water. They all had tall dragon heads and tails.
"In China there's a dragon boat festival every spring," said Dad.
"Why are all the boats shaped like dragons?" asked Grace.
"Long ago farmers believed that dragons would bring rain," said Dad. "Rice needs lots of rain to grow."
Just then Grace saw Peter with his team. He looked worried.
"One of our paddlers is sick," Peter said. "We can't race."
"I can paddle," said Grace.
"Thanks, Grace," Peter said. "But you don’t know how to paddle a dragon boat."
Grace shrugged. "I know how to row a canoe."
The boat captain heard Grace. "Let's give her a chance. The race starts in a few minutes!"
"Okay," Peter said.
Grace jumped into the boat. Peter gave her a paddle and showed her what to do. Then a horn blew. The dragon boats were off!
Boom! Boom! The captain stood in front with a drum. Each time she banged the drum, the twenty paddlers paddled. A boy in the back steered.
Boom! Whoosh! Boom! Whoosh!
The dragon boat flew over the water. The crowd roared from the shore.
Grace cheered as their boat zipped across the finish line.
"Third place!" cried Peter. "Thanks, Grace. You saved the day!"
It was a hot day. Nora opened the freezer and looked inside.
"Dad. There's no ice cream!" she complained.
Her father looked up from his computer. "Do you want to make some?"
"Homemade ice cream!" Nora cried. "Yes! Let's get started!"
Nora helped her father gather all the ingredients.
"Okay," Dad said. He was looking at a cookbook. "First we need egg yolks."
Crack! Nora broke some eggs and scooped out the yolks. She put them in a bowl. Dad added sugar. Then he whisked everything together.
Next Dad heated milk and vanilla in a pot. Then he slowly poured the liquid into the egg yolks. Nora stirred everything together.
They cooked the mixture until it got thick.
"Perfect," Dad said.
"What's next?" Nora asked.
"Now our mixture has to cool," Dad said.
Nora sighed. "Will it take a really long time?"
"Nope," said Dad. "Watch this." He put the pot in ice water.
"It's cooling fast!" Nora said.
"Yep." Dad took a cold container out of the freezer.
"What's that for?" Nora asked.
"It's for an ice cream machine," Dad said. "The machine will churn the mixture for us."
"Cool!" Nora said.
Dad showed Nora how to put the container into the machine. He poured in the mixture and Nora added heavy cream. Then they turned on the machine.
Twenty minutes later Dad turned it off. He covered the container and put it back into the freezer.
"Here comes the hard part," Dad said. "We wait!"
"Ugh," Nora groaned. "I hate waiting."
"Me too," said Dad. "So let's try to stay busy."
Dad and Nora played cards. They kicked a soccer ball around. They went for a long bike ride through the neighborhood.
Back at home Dad opened the freezer.
Nora stood behind him on tiptoes. "Is it ready?" she asked eagerly.
"Yes!" Dad said.
He scooped some ice cream and they tasted it.
"Mmm," Nora said, grinning. "I'm glad there was no ice cream in the freezer. Homemade ice cream is much better!"
Inez scanned the pool, looking for her friend. "Where's Odette?" she wondered.
Inez was with her cousin Angela. They had come to watch Odette's swim meet. Right now all the swimmers were warming up. But Inez couldn't find Odette anywhere.
"All the swimmers look the same," Inez complained. "Why do they all wear the same type of swimming gear?"

Angela laughed. "They all want to win! So they wear swimsuits and caps that help them move smoothly and quickly through the water. Swimsuit designers even use computer programs to make the gear more efficient."
Inez suddenly spotted her friend getting out of the pool. She waved. "Good luck, Odette!"

Odette waved back before joining her Bluefish teammates. The youngest swimmers stood near the edge of the pool, waiting for the first event to begin. Inez and Angela sat down on an empty bench as the horn blew.
"It's cool that you're on your college's swim team," Inez said. "I'd like to compete too."
"Why don't you try out for the Bluefish?" Angela asked.
Inez watched the swimmers shooting through the water. "Training seems hard. Besides, I love swimming, but I don't want to swim all day long!"
"Swimmers don't just train in the water," Angela said. "We exercise on land too. I go to the gym several times a week to lift weights."
"Oh. Do swimmers need to follow a certain diet?"

"Nutrition is important for any athlete," Angela said. "Before I train or compete, I eat very carefully. I eat carbohydrates for energy and protein to help my muscles. Our trainer creates meal plans for our team. We get to eat a lot of pasta!"
"I guess I could compete then," Inez said with a grin. "I'm very good at eating pasta! But I don't like going to bed early," she added. "Odette says she starts training at six in the morning."

"Many swimmers do train first thing in the morning—that's when pools are available. And all athletes need a good night's sleep. This helps us perform our best. Most swimmers try to get nine or ten hours of sleep each night."
Inez looked up. The next event was a relay. Odette stepped over to her lane. She was the first swimmer for the Bluefish.

The horn blew and the swimmers dived in. Splash! Odette hit the water and started swimming fast, easily pulling ahead of the other racers. She flipped at the wall and swam back. The next Bluefish swimmer dived in. All around the pool, people clapped and cheered.
"It does seem fun to swim on a team," Inez said.
"It is fun," Angela said. Then she nudged Inez. "So what do you think—will you try out for the Bluefish next year?"
"Um . . ." Inez thought for a minute and then nodded. "Yep, I think I'm ready to dive in!"
Election Day was coming up everywhere—even at my school. But I had a problem. My two best friends were running for school president! I could only vote for one of them.
Abby is really smart. She's my next-door neighbor. She moved here a couple years ago.
Matt is really popular. I've known him since kindergarten. We play on the same baseball team.
I helped them make campaign posters to hang in the school hallways. Matt and Abby both said, "Vote for me!"
But how could I choose between my best friends? Ugh! I wished there was no election.
"Why do we have to vote?" I asked Mrs. Hardy during social studies.
"Voting is a way for people to show their opinions," she explained. "Then decisions can be made based on the majority."
That didn't solve my problem.
I decided to ask my sister about voting. Becca turned 18 this year. She can vote in a real election for the first time.
"I can't wait to vote," she said. "Voting is a privilege!"
"Who are you voting for?" I asked.
"I'm not telling you." She stuck her tongue out at me. "Voting is private. That way people can feel free when they vote."
Downstairs, Mom and Dad were stuffing envelopes. They volunteer for Mayor Morgan's campaign. Even our front lawn is filled with campaign signs! Mom and Dad always say that elections are important.
"We pay taxes to the government," said Mom. "So we should choose good leaders."
"How do you know who to vote for?" I asked.
"Well," said Dad. "You have to think hard and know the facts."
"Voting isn't just marking a ballot," added Mom. "It's a serious responsibility. I vote for people who will make the world better for us."
My parents didn't solve my problem. But they had good advice.
I thought really hard about who to vote for. Abby wanted new classroom computers. Matt wanted to fix the baseball field. They both had good ideas. It wasn't easy, but finally I made a decision.

This morning at school, we voted. But I'm not saying who I voted for. Like Becca said, voting is private. The principal will announce the winner tomorrow. I know that he—or she!—will be a great school president.
I'm glad I answered my election question. But now I have a new problem! How will I cheer up the friend who doesn't win? Oh no!
It's early in the morning at 123 Dance Studio. Professional dancers are already in the practice rooms. Let's meet some of them!
Kira is a ballet dancer. She will audition for a role in The Nutcracker soon. That's a famous Russian ballet.
Ballet is difficult to learn. Ballet dancers must be flexible and strong. See how Kira stands on one foot and makes a full turn? She must hold her body really straight to do this turn.

Her shoes have flat front ends. The flat ends help her balance on the tips of her toes. Female ballet dancers often wear tutus for performances. These are short skirts with many layers. They let dancers move their legs freely.
Good luck with your audition, Kira!
Jay teaches hip-hop dance. He also creates dances for singers' music videos. He sometimes performs too. He's practicing a dance for today's class right now.

Jay's movements are quick and timed to the strong beats. Hip-hop dancers can use every part of their bodies. Jay dances in his everyday clothes and comfortable shoes. This helps him to move his body freely.
It looks like class is about to start. Let's move on.
Lisa and Mel are tap dancers. Tap dancers make loud taps on the floor with their feet.
They make these noises with special shoes. The bottoms of the shoes have metal plates at the heel and toe. When the metal hits the floor, it makes a loud noise.

Tap dance performances were popular in the early twentieth century. Back then tap dancers often performed to jazz. But now it can be performed to almost any kind of music. People still enjoy tap dance today.
Stomp! Stomp! Tap-tap! Lisa and Mel can tap fast!
Being a professional dancer is a difficult job. It takes years of training and hard work. But dancing is fun for everyone. Watch this!
My name is Mike. I play hockey. But I don't play ice hockey. I play a sport called sled hockey.
Do you know what sled hockey is? Let's go to the ice rink. I'll tell you more about this cool sport!
Sled hockey is for people with disabilities. It started in Sweden in the 1960s. Some men in wheelchairs invented it. They missed playing ice hockey. So they invented a new way to play.
In sled hockey, a player sits on a special sled. The sled has two metal blades. It works just like a big ice skate!

Sled hockey is a little different from ice hockey. Ice hockey players use one stick. But sled hockey players use two sticks. They are shorter than ice hockey sticks. Each stick has a pick at one end. These picks help players move across the ice. The other end has a wooden blade. The blade is for shooting the puck.
Otherwise, sled hockey is just like ice hockey. Each team has five players and a goalie. Players wear face masks, helmets, gloves, and pads. They shoot the puck into the net to score.
Today people play sled hockey all over the world. It's a very fast and fun game.
I'm ready to get on the ice. Watch this!
I skate . . . I shoot . . . I score!

22.title: How to Take Care of Your Bike

paragraphs.text: Do you love bike riding? I do. I ride my bike every day. It's important to take care of your bike. I'll show you how!
First, always check your bike's tires. You don't want to get a flat tire! So make sure your tires have enough air. This will protect the wheels too.
Second, oil the chain sometimes. This helps your chain last a long time. Get some bicycle oil. Turn one pedal with your hand. At the same time, drop oil on the chain. All you need is a few drops!

Third, keep your bike dry. Rain will make the metal parts rust. Keep your bike inside. If you must store it outside, get a cover for it. Sometimes your bike will get wet or muddy. Just wipe it as soon as you can.
Fourth, take your bike to a shop once a year. An expert can check your bike. Then you will know it's safe to ride. It's like seeing the doctor!
Oh, there's one more thing.
Check your seat height before you ride. Sit on the seat. Your feet should touch the ground. As you grow, you will need to raise the seat. I already raised mine twice!
My bike looks great. I'm ready to ride now. There's a new bike path in the park. I can't wait to try it!
Ella was getting ready for Christmas with her family. She was stringing brightly colored beads with her brother, Danny.
"Guess what?" Grandma called from the kitchen, where she was baking cookies. "It’s snowing!"
Howls of delight came from the children as they raced to look out the window.
"It’s going to be a white Christmas after all!" cried Ella.
"Hey, look who’s here!" said Danny, as Dad entered the room. He was covered with snow, holding up a tree.
"Now who is going to help me decorate this?" Dad asked with a grin.
Just then, Mom came downstairs carrying a big box of Christmas decorations.
"I think we’re going to need these," she said. Soon, everyone was in the spirit, helping to decorate the tree.
"It looks beautiful!" said Ella.
"Yes, I agree," Grandma said, "but I think it’s missing something extra special."
"Like what, Grandma?" asked Ella.
"Well, I’ve got some old ornaments, from when I was a little girl. I’ve been saving them to share with you, and I think the time has come."
Then she brought out a very old-looking box. "In here are my treasures from Christmas past. I have a story to tell about each ornament."
Everyone excitedly gathered around Grandma as she began.

"I remember the first time I walked into my hometown department store during Christmastime. I was amazed at the beautiful display trees, all different sizes and colors, all brightly lit. I felt as if I were in a magical fairyland. My mother asked me to help her pick out some ornaments for our tree. I picked out these," said Grandma as she held up two golden balls. She twirled them between her fingers. "I still love the way they sparkle."
"They look like little twinkling stars," said Ella admiringly.

"And here’s my sweet little angel," said Grandma, reaching into the box. "My grandfather gave me this one Christmas. I thought it was the most beautiful thing I’d ever seen. See her little wings? I asked my grandfather if she could fly. He said, ‘Yes, but only at night when we’re asleep.’" Grandma chuckled. "So I would sneak downstairs in the middle of the night, trying to catch her flying. I never did see her flying, but sometimes in my dreams I did!"
Ella laughed. "So you did see her fly! What’s next?"

"Now this one . . ." Grandma held up a blue dog with a bone in its mouth. "My favorite teacher gave me this. She was always making things and giving them to her students. Look at the way she painted the dog’s face, and on the back, she painted her name, Mrs. Beatty, and the year, 1944."
Ella looked thoughtful. "Your ornaments really are treasures, Grandma. How can you give them up?"

"Because I know you will treasure them as much as I do. Now this is the last ornament. I made this when I was in kindergarten. I remember how carefully I made it, gluing the wooden sticks together, letting the glue dry, then painting the whole thing white. It’s held up pretty well all these years, I must say." Grandma held the snowflake ornament in front of the window. Snow was falling gently outside.
Ella suddenly spoke up. "I have an idea! Why don’t we make our own ornaments?"
"That’s a wonderful idea, Ella," said Dad. "But how are we going to make them?"
"I know a recipe for making clay ornaments," said Grandma. "All we need is some flour, salt, and water. Then we cut the clay into shapes, bake our ornaments, and paint them."

So everyone got busy making ornaments. Dad made a car, Mom made a shoe, Danny made a football, and Grandma made a gingerbread man. Ella took the longest, but when she was finished, she surprised everyone.
"This is for you, Grandma," said Ella, "because you gave us your special ornaments." Ella made a snowflake with wings, put gold sparkles on it, and on the back, she had painted "Ella 2008."
Grandma was moved to tears. "Ella, this is the most beautiful Christmas ornament I’ve ever had. I will treasure it forever."
Ella gave Grandma a big hug. "And we will always treasure yours."
When do people in the United States make the most telephone calls? On what day do most people in the United States go out to eat?
The answer is Mother's Day, the second Sunday in May. On this day, sons and daughters thank their mothers for all their hard work and care.
Anna Jarvis is the woman who started Mother's Day in 1914.
Why? What was the real Mother's Day supposed to be about?
In the 1800s, the United States was fighting a civil war. Injured soldiers and many other people needed care.

In 1858, a woman from Pennsylvania named Ann Jarvis wanted to help. Ann Jarvis was the mother of Anna Jarvis. She organized women to provide medical care for soldiers and people affected by the war. The women volunteered in groups called Mothers' Day Work Clubs.
The clubs were neutral. They helped soldiers and their families on both sides of the war. Ann Jarvis and the Mothers' Day Work Clubs helped thousands of people to eat, live, and work safely.

Near the end of the war, Ann held a Mother's Friendship Day to bring everybody together in peace. Soldiers who had fought each other sat next to each other as friends. This day was so successful that it was repeated for many years after.
All her life, during wartime and peacetime, Ann Jarvis helped other people. After she died in 1905, her daughter Anna wanted her mother's good work to be remembered.

In 1908, Anna Jarvis held a church service to remember her mother. At the church, Anna handed people white carnations. These white carnations symbolized love and strengthㅡqualities which her mother had possessed.

Anna liked the church service very much. She decided to create a holiday to remember mothers everywhere. So, she promoted the idea to the government. Finally in 1914, President Wilson made Mother's Day a holiday.

Soon after, Mother's Day became very commercial. Selling things on Mother's Day became more important than its meaning. Florists and stores encouraged people to buy a card, a carnation, or a gift for Mother's Day. People forgot that they could just spend time with their mothers.
Anna Jarvis disliked this. She asked florists to stop selling flowers for Mother's Day, but they refused. Anna Jarvis spent many years reminding people of the true meaning of Mother's Day.
This Mother's Day, why don't you think about the real meaning of Mother's Day?
Do something special for your mother instead of simply buying a gift. You could do extra chores, go for a walk with her, or play her favorite music. That's what the real Mother's Day is about!

25.title: Art on the Streets of Bangladesh

paragraphs.text: Do you know where to find Bangladesh on a map? Most people have heard of it, but can't find it. We'll give you a hint: it is somewhere in Asia. Bangladesh is surrounded by India and a tiny part of Myanmar.

It is a small country, but it is a strong country. For hundreds of years, Bengalis have lived through many wars. And every year from May to October, the country is flooded by the monsoons and overflowing rivers. But the Bengalis have survived.
With the wars and the flooding, you might think the people are depressed. But they aren't.
The Bengalis like to say, "We don't have much, but we are proud of what we do have." If you visit Bangladesh, you will see that this is very true.

Everywhere you go in Bangladesh, the Bengalis show artistic pride in what they have. The women wear beautiful saris and salwar kameez . It takes eight and a half meters of fabric to make a sari , and the women wrap it around and around to make a dress.

It does not take as much fabric to make a salwar kameez , and the women say it is easy to wear. Both the sari and the salwar kameez are made out of bright and beautiful fabrics that give a feeling of life and happiness.

Believe it or not, the men actually wear skirts, called lungis . The lungi is made out of bright patterns and colors just like the women's clothes. And when they need to ride a bicycle or walk through deep water, they pull it up and tuck it in so that it looks like shorts.
For some people, all they own are the clothes they wear. But like all Bengalis, they show great pride by making their clothes very colorful.

Bengalis are also artistic when they travel. Because cars are so expensive, many Bengalis ride in rickshaws. A rickshaw is a bicycle with a cart behind it where one or two people ride inside. Of course, sometimes they can even squeeze three or four people inside!
Bengali rickshaw drivers are very proud of their rickshaws. Most rickshaws have been carefully decorated in bright colors on all sides.
If you rode in a rickshaw, you would see paintings on the back of the cart or its cover, on the driver's seat, and decorations on the wheels.
But, rickshaws aren't the only painted vehicles.

Those people who can afford trucks show how thankful they are by making them look beautiful. For example, this truck has five different pictures on each side. And that truck has different colored stripes on the front!
As you can see from our quick tour of Bangladesh, it is a very colorful country. And even though storms and battles may come, Bengalis still find a reason to be artistic and smile.

Every year on February 14th, couples, friends, and families in many countries give each other cards, chocolate, and candy. In fact over one billion cards are sent for this day, second only to Christmas.
Children have big parties at school, families send each other cards, and couples might have romantic dinners.
What do you do if you are single? Well Valentine's Day is not only for couples. It's about love, remember!

Valentine's Day is your chance to be bold. Is there a girl or boy that you secretly like? Why not send them a valentine? A valentine is a card with a message inside, like a poem or love letter. You can decide if you want to sign your name or not.

So where did the idea of Valentine's Day come from? In Italy about two thousand years ago, February 14th was a day to celebrate love. It was the day that the queen of the Roman gods, Juno, was honored. Juno was the god of women and marriage.

Young Roman women each wrote their name on a piece of paper and put it in a big jar. Every young man in the town picked a name. Then the pairs were partners until the next February. Sometimes they married.
At one time, however, young lovers in Italy could not marry. It was against the law! Why, you may ask? What could be wrong with people getting married?

Emperor Claudius II, the head of the Roman Empire in 270 AD, needed a big army because he fought many wars. He did not have enough soldiers. He believed single men were better soldiers than married men. If you are married and have a family, you may not want to leave your country and fight in a distant land. If you are single, you may like to join the army for an adventure!

Claudius needed more single men to be soldiers, and so he decided to outlaw marriage. People were angry, but they could do nothing. Claudius' nickname was Claudius the Cruel, and people who opposed him were usually killed.

One brave priest, whose name was Valentine, did oppose the emperor. Father Valentine married couples secretly in his church. He married many happy couples until one day he was caught. The Roman guards took him away and threw him in a dungeon. Emperor Claudius ordered his death.
While Valentine was in jail, he fell in love with the jailer's daughter. On the last day of his life, he sent her a love letter with the message, From your Valentine.

In 489 AD, Father Valentine was made a saint by the Christian Church, and St. Valentine's Day was declared on February 14th. Father Valentine's message, From your Valentine, is still written in many Valentine's Day cards today, 1,500 years later!
More importantly, Father Valentine's belief in the importance of love is still celebrated today between couples, families, and friends. Who will you send a valentine to?
Dogsledding─it's an exciting sport, but lots of hard work! That's Kerry's team over there. They are ready to start the race. Haze is the leader of the pack. He is an Alaskan husky.
Any type of dog can be a sled dog. Okay, almost any type; some are too small! Some popular sled dogs are Alaskan malamutes, Siberian huskies, and Eskimo dogs.
Sled dogs must be very strong. For example, look at Carmen. She can pull over 350 kilograms by herself!
"Okay, guys! Are you ready to run?" That's Kerry. He's the musher. The musher is the driver of the sled. It's very important for the musher and the pack to trust each other.
Mushers usually don't have trouble getting the dogs to pull the sled. Most of the time, it's hard to get the dogs to stop pulling!
Before a competition, the dogs train for months. Kerry trains his team by having them pull his car! "Come on, team! Faster, Haze!"
Since sled dogs train so hard, they need lots of food. A normal dog usually eats about 1,500 calories a day, or less. But sled dogs eat about ten thousand calories a day! That's a lot of food!
Although sled dogs are tough, they have sensitive feet. Kerry, the musher, ties booties on their feet. These booties protect the paws and keep them warm.
Each dogsled competition is different. Some teams have 16 dogs, while bigger ones have more than 200 dogs! Some races are short, while others are long. Some races last for days.
Sled dogs like cold, snowy days. They run faster and longer when there is snow. The snow is soft on their feet. And the cold weather keeps the dogs from getting too hot!
The mushers, like Kerry, must be strong leaders. If the musher gets tired or uncertain, the dogs sense it. Then the dogs begin to distrust the musher. That could be very dangerous.
Winning a dog-sled competition is very exciting. But it's not all about winning. It's about teamwork. It's about trust.
Dogsledding is about friendship. The best kind of friendship there is.
Hey, flag! Tell us about yourself!
"I am the Hinomaru, which means "sun disc." The sun disc, which is actually my red circle, has been the symbol of Japan for centuries. Many Japanese flags have used the sun disc.

"You may have seen a different flag in a war movie. It is called the Rising Sun. The Japanese navy used it during World War II. Some people think that it was the Japanese national flag during the war, but they are mistaken. The Rising Sun was only a military flag.
"I have been the Japanese flag for a long time.

"In the year 1274, the Mongols attacked Japan. Nichiren, a Japanese Buddhist priest, presented a sun flag to a very powerful Japanese warrior. He believed that with this symbol, the Japanese could defeat the Mongols. Ever since then, the sun disc has been an important symbol for the Japanese."
Hey, flag! Tell us about yourself.

"I am the flag of the People's Republic of China. I have been used since 1920, but I looked a little different back then. I got my new look in 1949. Red is the color of the Communist Revolution, which happened almost one hundred years ago. During the revolution, many people died to make China a communist country.
"In a communist country, the goal is for all the people to be treated equally and for them to share all the wealth. So the Chinese people are proud of my red color.

"I have five yellow stars. The large star represents the Communist Party of China. The Communist Party leads all the Chinese people. The four small stars represent the Chinese people. Some people say that the small stars represent the workers, farmers, scholars, and business owners. The five stars show that all the people are united under the Communist Party."
Hey, flag! Tell us about yourself.

"I am the flag of the Republic of Korea. You can call me the Taegeukgi. I have looked like this since 1950, but other flags similar to me have been used by Korean kings for hundreds of years. Many hundreds of years ago, my colors were very different. In 1882, I looked almost the same as I do now. Can you see the differences?

"My design and colors have changed, but my meaning remains the same. It comes from a very old oriental philosophy. The circle in the center is a symbol of eum-yang , which the Chinese people call yin-yang .The blue part represents eum , which is negative, dark, and cold. The red part represents yang , which is positive, bright, and hot. Together, they symbolize balance and harmony.
"The bar on my top-left side means the sky; the one on the top-right means water; the bottom-left one means fire; and the bottom-right one means the earth.
"Most importantly, I am not a flag of war, but one that stands for peace and harmony. Even my white background represents peace and purity.
"If you want to know about the history of a country, start by learning about its flag. A flag can speak a thousand words."
October 27th, 28th, 29th, 30th, 31st—oh no! There are only five more days until Halloween, and we’re not ready. But we won’t panic: we just need a good plan.
Today Dad will drive us to the pumpkin patch. We will search and search. We’ll see pumpkins that are too small. We won’t want those.
We will also see pumpkins that are funny shaped. We won’t want those either. We will search for the perfect pumpkin.
On the twenty-eighth, Mom will help us carve the pumpkin. We will take out the seeds and slimy stuff. Mom will bake the seeds for us. Mmm!
We’ll cut out scary eyes, a pointy nose, and a mouth with teeth. When we are finished, we’ll have a jack-o’-lantern. He’ll be scary!

On the twenty-ninth, we will put up the decorations. We will make witches, moons, black cats, and scary bats. Then we’ll put them in our front windows and door. Dad will bring home a big bundle of hay, and Mom will sit the scarecrow on it. Then Dad will put a red lightbulb over the door. That will really make our house spooky.

On the thirtieth, we will make our costumes. I’m going to be a pirate. I’ll have a patch over my eye, a long sword, and a hook for my left hand. My sister will be a mummy. We will wrap her in white cloth from head to toe. The last things we will need are two baskets for our candy.

October 31st is Halloween. After dinner we will quickly put on our costumes. Mom will paint a black beard on my face. Then Dad will take us out to trick-or-treat. We will have to walk fast because there are so many houses to visit. At each house we will knock on the door and say, "Trick or treat."
After a long night of trick-or-treating, we will bring home our baskets of candy. Mom likes chocolate, so we can give her some. Dad likes peanuts, so we can give him those.
That is our Halloween plan. Let’s go to the pumpkin patch!
In the 1930s, Adolf Hitler became the leader of Germany. He was a very evil man and committed many horrible crimes against the people of Europe. In 1940, he attacked the peaceful nation of Holland.
The people of Holland, called the Dutch, were forced to become part of Germany. They had to live under German law and do whatever the German soldiers told them to do.
If the German soldiers wanted their food or blankets, they had to give them up.

After the Germans defeated the Dutch, the queen of Holland had to leave the country. Queen Wilhelmina , her daughter, and granddaughters all escaped to London. But London was not very safe either. Hitler and his army were bombing London every night.

So, Queen Wilhelmina sent her daughter, Princess Juliana, and her granddaughters to live in Ottawa, the capital city of Canada. In Ottawa, the Canadian people took very good care of the princess and her daughters.
However, Queen Wilhelmina did not come to Canada. Even though it was very dangerous, she stayed in London. She would send radio messages to the people of Holland. She would tell them not to give up.
In Ottawa, Princess Juliana had a baby girl. To celebrate, the Canadians raised the Dutch flag and played the Dutch national anthem. It was a wonderful feeling for the princess.
The queen heard about the celebration and announced the exciting news on her radio broadcast. When the people of Holland heard this news, they were very thankful to the Canadians.

Then, in 1944, the Canadian soldiers came to Holland and helped defeat the German army. The people of Holland were even more grateful for this. The people wanted to thank the Canadians for taking care of their princess and for helping defeat Hitler's army.
Princess Juliana presented the city of Ottawa with 100,000 tulip bulbs.
Holland is famous for its beautiful tulips. The country is covered with tulips every spring. So, the gift of tulips to Canada was a true sign of friendship.
Tulips grow in the early spring and then die just before summer. But the tulip bulbs do not die. They stay in the earth. Every spring they blossom into beautiful new tulips again.
Every year, the Queen of Holland sends 10,000 more tulips to Ottawa. Now, after more than fifty years of sending them, Ottawa is full of tulips. Every spring, Ottawa celebrates with a festival.
The Canadian Tulip Festival is the largest tulip festival in the world.
The city of Ottawa is not only the capital city of Canada, it is also the capital city of tulips.
Princess Juliana, who became Queen Juliana, attended the tulip festival during a royal visit in 1967. The tulips in Ottawa have become a beautiful sign of the friendship between these two countries.
Spring is the season of new beginnings. Flowers and trees come back to life after the long winter. Spring is also the time to celebrate Easter.
For Christians, Easter is a religious holiday. Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead three days after he was killed. Easter is a holiday to celebrate Jesus' resurrection.
Today, however, Christians are not the only people who celebrate Easter.
Where does the word "Easter" come from? What do the bunnies and eggs have to do with Easter?
The word "Easter" comes from a goddess named Eostre. Ancient people held a festival to worship Eostre every spring. Her symbol was a rabbit.
Eostre, or Easter, and the rabbit both symbolize fertility. Fertility means having lots and lots of babies. So the Easter rabbit represents new life.
The egg is also a symbol of fertility and new life. There are many customs and traditions associated with eggs. Some cultures even believe that the Earth hatched from a giant egg!
Easter eggs are painted bright colors. These colors represent spring.

In Greece, Easter eggs are colored red. Red represents Jesus' blood. In some parts of Germany and Austria, people color their eggs green. In Russia and Ukraine, people decorate their eggs in beautiful patterns with gold and silver.
On Easter day some countries have egg-rolling competitions. The egg that rolls the farthest wins. But the most popular Easter game is the Easter egg hunt.

Children believe the Easter Bunny brings the eggs during the night. On Easter morning, the children look for the eggs. Sometimes there is a prize for the child who finds the most eggs. Everyone has a good time.
Easter is a fun time for the whole family. It is a time to celebrate life.
Hello! Welcome to our St. Patrick's Day parade! We have lots of fun on St. Patrick's Day. Do you know what St. Patrick's Day is?
St. Patrick was born in Britain. His family was very rich. When St. Patrick was 16 years old, something terrible happened.
A group of pirates attacked St. Patrick's home. Then they kidnapped the young man and took him to Ireland. The pirates sold St. Patrick as a slave.

St. Patrick spent six years as a slave. He worked as a shepherd. Being far away from his family made St. Patrick feel sad and lonely. But St. Patrick prayed every day. His faith grew stronger and stronger.
One day, St. Patrick heard a voice telling him to run away. So St. Patrick listened to the voice. He escaped and went to France. In France, St. Patrick became a priest.
When St. Patrick was about sixty years old, he returned to Ireland. He wanted to tell the Irish about his faith. Almost everybody loved Patrick.
He carried a shamrock with him. A shamrock is a three-leaf clover. St. Patrick used a shamrock to teach people about God.
According to legend, St. Patrick drove out all the snakes in Ireland. Snakes were a symbol of evil. St. Patrick wanted to remove all evil from Ireland.
When St. Patrick died, the people of Ireland were very sad. They decided to honor his death. That's how St. Patrick's Day began.
Can you guess why we are all wearing green? Green is the color of spring! Since St. Patrick died in the spring, we wear green to show that we honor him.
A four-leaf clover, that's a sign of good luck! On St. Patrick's Day, it is good luck to find a four-leaf clover.
As for me, I'm a leprechaun. I am part of St. Patrick's Day because I am Irish too! Now that you know about St. Patrick's Day, why don't you join our fun?
"Who will be my valentine?" Caroline wondered. She needed to choose soon—Valentine's Day was the next day! "Maybe I should choose Tommy," she thought. "Or perhaps I should choose Tyler!"
"Put your books away. It's time for art," Miss Smith said to the whole class. "Today we are making Valentine's cards."
"Tommy or Tyler, who will it be," wondered Caroline. "Maybe if I cut out a big red heart, my heart will help me choose."

Caroline cut out a red paper heart. When she finished, the heart began to hum. Then, it jumped up and began to sing, "I am your Valentine's heart. I am really smart! Write a poem to the one you love the best. And I will sing, dance, and do the rest!"

Caroline wrote her poem. It was lovely and sweet, but she still didn't know who to give her Valentine's Day heart to. Caroline added white lace and a small red bow to her heart. Her heart looked pretty, but still she wondered, "Tommy or Tyler, who should I choose? Who will receive my Valentine's Day heart?"
The next day was Valentine's Day—February 14! The classroom was decorated in pink and white. The children giggled happily.

"Now it is time to give your Valentine's heart away," said Miss Smith. Miss. Smith had hung a red curtain in the classroom. She separated the boys and girls. Each stood on a different side of the curtain.

Caroline's heart beat as she stepped to her side of the curtain. She still had not chosen her valentine. Then to her surprise, her Valentine's Day heart began to spell out a name. Letters appeared on her heart and spelled out " T–y–l–e–r ."
"Tyler! Come and be my Valentine," called Caroline.
Tyler sprang from behind the red curtain. Caroline gave him a hug and her Valentine's Day heart.
All day Caroline and Tyler sat together. At recess Tyler pushed Caroline on the swing.
And the Valentine's Day heart sang, "Valentine's Day, Valentine's Day, what a happy day to play! I really hope to hear you say, ‘I love you,' on this happy Valentine's Day!"
It is almost Christmas. Today the Smith family is going to get their Christmas tree.
"Come on, Jay and Sarah. Let’s get going," says Dad.
"Where are we going, Dad?" asks Jay.
"We’re going to the Christmas tree farm."
Jay and Sarah are excited. "All right!" they cheer.
When the Smith family arrives at the tree farm, they see thousands of Christmas trees.
"Look at all the trees. They are planted in straight rows," says Sarah.
"They have many kinds of Christmas trees," Dad says.
"Yes," says Mom, "those are white pines. And these are spruce trees."
Picking a tree is not easy. Some trees are too small. Some trees are too big. Some trees are not straight.
"How about this tree?" says Jay, pointing.
"It’s too thin, Jay," Dad says.
"What about that tree?" suggests Sarah.
Mom disagrees. "It’s too twisty, Sarah." Then Mom finds a tall, straight tree. "I like that tree. It is a perfect Christmas tree."
"Wow! I like it too," says Jay.
"It’s beautiful," says Sarah.
Dad agrees. "Let’s cut it down." With a chain saw, he cuts through the trunk of the tree. "Timber!"
"Stay back, Jay. It’s going to fall," warns Mom.
Mom and Dad go to pay for the tree, and Sarah and Jay enjoy a hot cup of apple cider. The tree farm makes delicious hot apple cider. Soon, it is time to go.
"Thank you very much. Enjoy your tree," says the man at the tree farm.
"Merry Christmas," the Smiths say.
In the parking lot, they tie their new Christmas tree to the roof of the car. Then they drive home.
Cutting down the tree is only half the fun. When they get home, it is time to decorate it.
"Brush the snow off the tree," says Mom.
"I’ll get the Christmas tree stand," says Dad. Dad puts the tree into the stand. Without the stand, the tree cannot stand up. "Now we can decorate the tree."
"First we must put the lights on," says Mom.
Sarah makes sure that every lightbulb works. Dad and Jay put the lights on the tree.
"Look at this one. It’s pretty," says Sarah.
"The tin soldiers are my favorite," says Jay.
"Now, Jay and Sarah," says Mom, "you can put some tinsel on the tree."
When they are done, Sarah is pleased. "Wow, it looks beautiful."
The tree is almost finished. It looks great, but there is one thing missing. "The star!" says Mom.
No Christmas tree is complete without a star on top. Dad lifts Jay up so that he can place the star on the top of the tree.
"Perfect!" says Mom.
"This is the greatest Christmas tree ever," says Sarah. And everyone agrees!
Children around the world have different birthday parties. What do they do?
Hi! I am from Argentina. At my birthday party, my family and friends pull on my ear seven times because I am seven years old.
Hi! I am from China. At my birthday party, my family and friends eat noodles together and wish me a long life.
Hi! I am from Denmark. At my birthday party, my cake is decorated with the Danish flag.
Hi! I am from England. For my birthday party, my mother bakes a cake with coins in it. If I find a coin in my piece, I will grow up to be rich.
Hi! I am from India. On my birthday, I wear a colorful dress to school. My best friend gives out chocolates to my friends.
Hi! I am from Israel. At my birthday party, the grown-ups lift me up into the air and put me back down again.
Hi! I am from Korea. At my birthday party, my mother serves seaweed soup and rice cakes. My family and friends all eat together.
Hi! I am from Mexico. At my birthday party, I wear a blindfold and hit a piñata until it breaks open. Then, we all share the candy inside.
Hi! I am from the Philippines. Before my birthday party, I go to church with my family to pray.
Hi! I am from the United States. At my birthday party, I make a wish and blow out the candles on my birthday cake. If I blow them all out, my wish will come true.
